document.title: -OLIGOGLUCAN :ORTHOPHOSPHATE GLUCOSYLTRANSFERASES FROM EUGLENA GRACILIS I, ISOLATION AND SOME PROPERTIES OF A fl-I,3-OLIGOGLUCAN PHOSPHORYLASE 4r7
document.abstract: i. A new enzyme has been found in cell free extracts of Euglena gracilis which catalyzes the reversible phosphorolytic cleavage of/~-I,3-oligoglucans according to the following reaction: (~-I,3-glucose)n + Pi,~ (~-I,3-glucose)n-: + a-D-glucose 1-phosphate

method.heading: Methods
method.text:
Pi was determined by the method of FISKE AND SUBBARow a and Glc-I-P either by the measurement of labile Pi (0.5 M H2SO a for 5 min at IOO °) or with the phosphoglucomutase-Glc-6-P dehydrogenase-NADP system 4.
Reducing power was measured according to SOMOGYI 5 and NELSON6; hexose was estimated by the phenol-HaSO 4 methodL Degree of polymerization of oligosaccharides was determined as described by PEAT, WHELAN AND ROBERTS s. Glucose was determined with glucose oxidase and peroxidase but substituting 0.4 M Tris-HC1 buffer, pH 7.6, for o.I M acetate buffer, pH 5-4 (ref. 9) or by the procedure of CAPUTTO, LELOIR AND TRUCCO 10 which minimizes interferences with reducing oligosaccharides.
Protein was estimated by the method of LowRY et al. 1~.
Chromatography was carried out on Whatman No. I or washed Whatman No. 3 MM paper. When the latter was used, a piece of Whatman No. i paper was sewed at the top of the sheet.
The solvent systems used were: (i) butanol-pyridine-water (6:4:3, by vol.); (2) propanol--ethyl acetate-water (7 :I :2, by vol.).
Previous to the chromatographic runs, the enzymatic reaction products were desalted by passing through a column of Amberlite mixed-bed resin (acetate form) and the percolate was concentrated either in a vacuum or on a boiling-water bath.
Paper electrophoresis of sugars was performed on Whatman No. i paper with 0.05 M potassium borate for 2 h at 20 V/cm or with 2% sodium molybdate, pH 5.1, as described by BOURNE, HUTSON AN/) WEIGEL 1~, for 75 min at 25 V/cm. Sugar spots were visualized according to TREVELYAN, PROCTER AND HARRISON 13.

method.heading: Materials
method.text:
The materials were the same as in the earlier paper 1 except for those listed below.
Calcium phosphate gel (20 g dry weight per 1) was prepared according to KEILIN AND HARTREE 14.

method.heading: Preparation of glycosides. Laminaribiosyl-and laminaritriosyl-hydroquinone
method.text:
were prepared by incubation of the enzyme preparation ("33-66% ammonium sulfate step", see below) with 20 mM arbutin, 2o mM Glc-l-P, 4 ° mM imidazole buffer, pH 6.5, and I mM EDTA for I h. After desalting as described above, the hydroquinone glycosides were isolated by chromatography with Solvent I and on washed Whatman No. 17 paper sewed to Whatman No. I paper.
Laminaribiosyl-, laminaritriosyl-and laminaritetraosyl-saligenin were prepared and isolated in the same manner but using salicin instead of arbutin in the incubation mixture.
The hydroquinone derivatives were identified as described before I and those corresponding to saligenin were tentatively recognized as follows. Laminaritriosyland laminaribiosyl-saligenin were partially hydrolyzed with 0.5 M acetic acid during 4 h, chromatographed on Whatman No. I paper in Solvent I and revealed with AgNO~. Three and two spots were respectively detected which corresponded to the standards of laminaritriose, laminaribiose and glucose in the first case, and laminaribiose and glucose in the second. In addition, the RF of the products and those of the original phenolic glucosides were determined in Solvents I and 2. A plot of log (I/RF--I) against the number of hexose units 1~ gave a linear relationship, indicating that the compounds belonged to a homologous series. This was the only criterion used to identify laminaritetraosyl-saligenin due to scarcity of material.

method.heading: Procedure B
method.text:
(I) Preincubation mixture. It was similar to that described above except that 2 #moles of potassium phosphate buffer, pH 7.2, was used instead of imidazole buffer and that the amount of enzyme was lowered to 0.005-0.02 units.
(2) Incubation mixture. Laminaritriose (0. 5/,mole) was added to the preincubation mixture and after IO rain of incubation at 37 °, the GIc-I-P formed was determined, after heating 2 min at IOO °, by the phosphoglucomutase-Glc-6-P dehydrogenase-NADP system.
Controls were carried out similarly but omitting the trisaccharide. One unit of enzyme is defined as that amount catalyzing the formation of I/,mole of Pi per min under the conditions described in Procedure A.

method.heading: Preparation and isolation of laminaritriose labeled with [14C] glucose at the ]]O11-reducing end,
method.text:
Step 2 Hydrolysis of laminaritriose and isolation of lamhlaribiose labeled with radioactive glucose at the non-reducing end.
Step 3
Reduction with sodium borohydride and identification of the product formed by electrophorests.
Step 4 was prepared and preincubated as under Enzyme assay, Procedure A. Then 5/,moles of laminaribiose and 5.3/,moles of E14ClGlc-I-P (26 400 counts/min per/,mole) were added in a final vol. of o.I ml and incubated at 37 ° for I h. The reaction was stopped by heating and after desalting and concentrating as described under Methods, the percolate was spotted on Whatman No. 3 MM paper and chromatographed with Solvent I during 20 h. Then the paper was dried and rechromatographed in the same solvent for another 20 h. A scanning for radioactivity was made and the area corresponding to the trisaccharide was cut out and eluted with water. Approx. 0.8/,mole of the sugar with a specific activity of 25 ooo counts/min per #mole was obtained.

A previous paper from this laboratory 1 dealt with laminaribiose phosphorylase, an enzyme isolated from Euglena gracilis strain z which catalyzes the reaction: Further work has shown that extracts of the same organism contain another enzyme which catalyzes the same reaction but differs in several properties. As will be reported in the following paper 2, both enzymes can be separated by column chromatography. The new enzyme phosphorolyzes laminaritriose and higher homologues at a greater rate than laminaribiose, while the opposite behavior is observed with laminaribiose phosphorylase. Furthermore, the two enzymes differ in their requirement for compounds with -SH groups; this effect is especially observed in aged enzyme preparations. The new enzyme shows an absolute requirement for -SH bearing compounds while laminaribiose phosphorylase is only slightly activated.
The name fi-I,3-oligoglucan :orthophosphate glucosyltransferase II is proposed for the new enzyme and fi-I,3-oligoglucan:orthophosphate glucosyltransferase I for the previously reported laminaribiose phosphorylase. The trivial name fl-I,3-oligoglucan phosphorylase for the new enzyme is used in this and in the following paper 2.
The present communication reports the isolation of the fl-I,3-oligoglucan phosphorylase, its specificity and some of its kinetic parameters. The next paper 2 deals with comparative studies of the two phosphorylases.

Two assays were used to determine the fl-I,3-oligoglucan phosphorylase reaction. Procedure A was used to determine the enzyme activity on reaction (I) from right to left and procedure B to measure the phosphorolytic activity.
Procedure A (~) Preincubation mixture. 2/zmoles of imidazol buffer, pH 7.2, o.2/~mole of EDTA, I/,mole of mercaptoethanol and enzyme (o.oi to 0.04 unit, see below), in a volume of 0.o3 ml, were preincubated at 3 °0 for 30 min.
(2) Incubation mixture. Laminaribiose* (0.5/,mole) and I #mole of Glc-I-P (dipotassium salt) were added to the preincubation mixture and incubated at 37 ° for io rain; the final vol. was 0.05 ml. The reaction was stopped by 4o-fold dilution with water and the released Pi was determined. Controls were prepared similarly but omitting the acceptor. This procedure was used in most experiments of the present study.
(I) Preincubation mixture. It was similar to that described above except that 2 #moles of potassium phosphate buffer, pH 7.2, was used instead of imidazole buffer and that the amount of enzyme was lowered to 0.005-0.02 units.
(2) Incubation mixture. Laminaritriose (0. 5/,mole) was added to the preincubation mixture and after IO rain of incubation at 37 °, the GIc-I-P formed was determined, after heating 2 min at IOO °, by the phosphoglucomutase-Glc-6-P dehydrogenase-NADP system.

Cells of Euglena gracilis strain z were grown under natural light at room temperature (24-300) * and processed as described previously 1 up to the "33-66% ammonium sulfate step". Table I summarizes the results obtained in a typical experiment, starting from I 1 of culture medium (approx. 15 ml of green wet cells).
The ammonium sulfate fraction (12 ml) was treated with enough calcium phosphate gel (5 mg of the gel/mg protein) to adsorb most of the protein. After standing for io min in an ice bath, with occasional stirring, the mixture was centrifuged at IO ooo × g for IO min and the enzyme was eluted from the gel with sodium pyrophosphate as described in Table I. At each step the suspension was allowed to stand in the cold, with occasional stirring, for IO min and was centrifuged as above. All the eluates were separately dialyzed overnight against i 1 of io mM Tris buffer, (pH 7.2)-1 mM EDTA, with one change of the liquid.
Table I shows that Fractions I and II were enriched with laminaribiose phosphorylase while the new enzyme was ehited from the gel with Io mM sodium pyrophosphate. Occasionally, however, /5-I,3-oligoglucan phosphorylase appeared after the third elution with 5 mM sodium pyrophosphate.
In most of the experiments mentioned in this paper, Fraction IV was used as fl-I,3-oligoglucan phosphorylase. The highest purification achieved was about Io-fold from the crude extract to the last fraction.
Table I shows that, under the described conditions, laminaribiose phosphorylase (Fractions I and II) catalyzed the Pi released from Glc-I-P at a rate IO-2o-fold lower with laminaribiose than with glucose as acceptor. On the other hand, fi-I,3oligoglucan phosphorylase (Fractions III to V) liberated Pi from the phosphoric ester at similar rates using either the monosaccharide or the disaccharide as substrate (last column of Table I). These ratios of activities were consistently observed in different preparations, including in the enzymes separated by DEAE-cellulose column chromatography 2. In most of the experiments described in the present paper, laminaribiose was used as acceptor. Thus, the possible contamination of the new enzyme with some laminaribiose phosphorylase cannot affect the results since, according to the amount of enzyme used, the Pi released due to the action of the disaccharide phosphorylase is within the experimental error. Obviously, as can be seen also in Table I, this reasoning cannot be applied when glucose was the acceptor, due to the fact that both enzymes act on the later sugar with similar velocities.
The stability was somewhat variable in different batches. 2-and 8-week-old extracts showed an apparent loss of activity of 80 and over 95%, respectively, when assayed without mercaptoethanol during the preincubation. When the latter step was carried out with -SH containing compounds (see Enzyme assay), about 50% of the original activity was recovered in 8-week-old preparations.
A linear relationship was obtained between the Pi released and time or enzyme concentration when the activity of fl-I,3-oligoglucan phosphorylase was measured as described under Enzyme assay, Procedure A.
Table II shows the Km and Vmax. of various acceptors. It can be seen that while the Vmax. was similar for all of the sugars tested, the Km for glucose was about IO-2o-fold higher than for fl-i,3-oligoghicans. The Km found for glucose was approx. twice that determined with laminaribiose phosphorylase, but at variance with the latter ~, higher concentrations of glucose were not inhibitory.

In all cases, initial reaction rates were used to determine the Kin. was found to be 3 and 2 mM with laminaritetraose (13 raM) or laminaritriose (IO mM) as glucosyl donor, respectively" that of Glc-I-P was 1.8 mM when laminaribiose (IO mM) was used as acceptor.
Fig. I shows the effect of pH on the reaction rate with glucose or laminaribiose as acceptor. The optimal pH obtained with both substrates ranged from 7 to 7.5.
The effect of pH on the initial velocity when laminaritetraose, laminaritriose and laminaribiose were used as glucosyl donors to form Glc-I-P is shown in Fig. 2 The highest activity for the three substrates was obtained at about pH 7.2. It should be noted that the reaction is slower with laminaribiose than with laminaritriose and laminaritetraose, so that six times as much enzyme had to be used in order to obtain similar amounts of Glc-I-P. Two possibilities may explain this result: the first is that the preparation of/5-1,3-oligoglucan phosphorylase was contaminated with some laminaribiose phosphorylase. The other is that the reaction rate of the former enzyme with laminaribiose is about 6-fold lower than with the other oligosaccharides. Although at this time it is not easy to discard the possibility of contamination, the results presented in the next paper 2 support the second explanation.
On the other hand, and although this is not conclusive evidence, the fact that the activity profile as a function of pH was the same for the three sugars, suggests that only one enzyme is involved in the reaction.
When/5-I,3-oligoglucan phosphorylase was incubated for 15 min or more under standard conditions with laminaribiose as acceptor, a series of reducing substances with RF corresponding to those of laminaritriose and higher oligosaccharides, up to at least laminariheptaose, as well as glucose, were detected by paper chromatography. A similar pattern was observed when IO or 20 mM glucose was substituted for laminaribiose.
In order to identify the first higher homologue of laminaribiose formed by enzyme action, the following steps were carried out (see Fig. 3).

Step 2 Hydrolysis of laminaritriose and isolation of lamhlaribiose labeled with radioactive glucose at the non-reducing end.
Step 3
Reduction with sodium borohydride and identification of the product formed by electrophorests.
Step 4 was prepared and preincubated as under Enzyme assay, Procedure A. Then 5/,moles of laminaribiose and 5.3/,moles of E14ClGlc-I-P (26 400 counts/min per/,mole) were added in a final vol. of o.I ml and incubated at 37 ° for I h. The reaction was stopped by heating and after desalting and concentrating as described under Methods, the percolate was spotted on Whatman No. 3 MM paper and chromatographed with Solvent I during 20 h. Then the paper was dried and rechromatographed in the same solvent for another 20 h. A scanning for radioactivity was made and the area corresponding to the trisaccharide was cut out and eluted with water. Approx. 0.8/,mole of the sugar with a specific activity of 25 ooo counts/min per #mole was obtained.
Step 2" Obtaining of 14C-labeled disaccharide. Approximately one half of the 14Clabeled sugar obtained in the previous step was diluted with 2/~moles of cold laminaritriose and submitted to a partial hydrolysis in o.165 M H~SO 4 for I h at IOO °. The hydrolysate was neutralized with Ba(OH)2. The BaSO, formed was removed by centrifugation and discarded after washing with water.
The supernatant fluid and the washings were pooled, concentrated, spotted on Whatman No. 3 MM paper, and chromatographed for 40 h in Solvent I.
After automatic scanning for radioactivity, the area corresponding to the 14C-labeled disaccharide was cut out and eluted with water.
Step 3: Reduction of labeled disaccharide. A carrier of unlabeled laminaribiose (2 #moles) was mixed with the radioactive disaccharide, and sodium borohydride, in a final concn, of o.7~ o was added. The mixture was allowed to stand for I h at room temperature and the remaining borohydride was decomposed by adding two drops of 5 M HC1. The mixture was then evaporated 3 or 4 times in a vacuum, in the presence of methanol. After desalting, the reduced 14C-labeled disaccharide (laminaribiitol (G-S)) was submitted to paper electrophoresis in sodium molybdate as described in Methods. The scanning for radioactivity showed only one peak with a Msorbitol ~ 0.I. Under the described conditions, sorbitol ran about 17 cm; no correction was made for electro-osmosis. According to BOURNE, HUTSON AND WEIGEL 16, 2-, 4-and 6-O-substituted D-glucitol will form a complex with molybdate while the 3-O-substituted isomer will not. Hence, only the latter derivative will remain immobile by ionophoresis in molybdate. This result permits one to assign to the reduced disaccharide a 1,3-bond.
Step 4: Hydrolysis of the reduced disaccharide. In order to confirm that the product formed in Step 3 was laminaribiitol, the radioactive band of the ionophoreto gram was eluted with water and desalted as described before. The percolate was hydrolyzed in i M HC1 at ioo ° for I h. Subsequently, it was dried under vacuum, neutralized with pyridine and again run in electrophoresis as mentioned in Step 3. By scanning, a radioactive peak ~ith a Msorbitol <~ O.I was again observed. This zone was cut out and eluted with water. The rest of the paper strip was visualized according to TREVELYAN, PROCTER AND HARRISON 1~ and a spot running as sorbitol was detected. The eluted radioactive material was desalted as above and then submitted to paper electrophoresis in sodium tetraborate. An automatic scanning of the paper strip showed a radioactive band with a Mglueose of I.
As mentioned before, these results demonstrate the existence of a 1,3-bond between the two non-reducing glucoses of the trisaccharide. As the latter was obtained from laminaribiose, it can be designated as a glucosyl-I,3-glucosyl /5-1, 3glucose.

The higher oligosaccharides formed by the latter enzyme were identified as laminaritetraose, laminaripentaose, laminarihexaose and laminariheptaose, by comparison with a paramylon hydrolysate in paper chromatography with Solvents I and 2. Moreover, a plot of --log RG against the number of glucose units according to JOHNSTON 17 gives a linear relationship, thus indicating that they were oligosaceharides of the same r-I,3 series.
Table IV shows the stoichiometry of the reaction. It can be observed that the disappearance of Glc-I-P and laminaribiose agree with the formation of Pi and higher oligosaccharides, respectively. In Expt. I (IO min incubation), a small but significant amount of laminaripentaose was formed while in Expt. 2 (80 min) laminarihexaose could also be detected. Values in parentheses correspond to/~moles of glucosyl residues originated from Glc-I-P. A good agreement between the sum of these values and that of Pi liberation can be seen. a-Glc-I-P is quite specific as donor of the glucose moiety; the following sugar phosphates were ineffective: a-Man-l-P, a-Gal-I-P, /~-Glc-I-P and Fru-I,6-P~. On the other hand, besides glucose, several/~-substituted glucosides may act as acceptors, as shown in Table V.
By comparison of the results shown in the table with those previously reported for laminaribiose phosphorylase 1, one can observe a qualitative similarity in acceptor specificity. However, the enzymes differ from the quantitative point of view. Thus, when the rates of Pi released by laminaribiose phosphorylase using glucose as acceptor were taken as ioo%, the values for most of the other sugars was below 25~o.
When/5-I,3-oligoglucan phosphorylase was incubated with arsenate and/%I, 3glucosyl oligosaccharides, a cleavage of the sugars was detected. The values corresponding to the reducing power liberated after 20 min incubation, expressed as glucose, are shown in Table VI. No glucose could be detected when KOH-treated paramylon TM or laminarin was used as substrate. This result together with the fact
The preincubation mixture was as follows: 2/,moles of imidazole buffer, pH 7.2; o.2 #*mole ot EDTA, I #mole of mercaptoethanol and o.oi ml of Fraction IV (see Table I) in a total vol. oi o.o 3 ml. After 3 ° min preincubation at 3 o°, the substrates in the concentrations indicated below and i/~mole of potassium arsenate, pH 7.2, in a final vol. of 0.05 ml were added and incubated at 37 ° for 20 min. Reducing power was determined by the method of CAPUTTO, LELOIR AND TRUCCO TM. Controls were carried out by addition of substrates at the end of the incubation. that the polysaccharide did not serve as acceptor (Table V) indicates a certain specificity towards the glucosyl chain length. On the other hand, no arsenolysis of Glc-I-P could be observed in the absence of acceptor. This behavior is similar to that of maltose, cellobiose 19 and laminaribiose phosphorylases 1. This finding might indicate that no glucosyl-enzyme intermediate is formed and that the reaction occurs by a single displacement mechanism. that the difference between the presence and absence of mercaptoethanol was about I3-fold. This difference was usually obtained with enzymes about 2 months old. In addition, glutathione and cysteine, at a concn, of 20 mM could reactivate the enzyme to the same extent as mercaptoethanol, while EDTA was ineffective. This finding would indicate that the enzyme reactivation was not due to the chelating effect of the sulfhydryl compounds, but to their reducing power.
On the other hand, the preincubation time required for optimal enzyme reactivation at 3 °° was approx. 15-3o min, at 20 mM of mercaptoethanol.
Neither activation nor inactivation was observed by adding the following compounds to the standard reaction mixtures: 2 mM UDP, UDP-Glc, CDP, ITP, ATP, ADP, sodium pyrophosphate, 5 mM AMP, o.oi mM cyclic 3',5'-AMP and 4 mM hydroquinone. However, when mercaptoethanol was omitted from the standard incubation mixture using fresh enzyme preparations, 4 mM hydroquinone inhibited 80% and 90% of the original activity with glucose or laminaribiose as acceptor, respectively.
When the enzyme was assayed in the direction of phosphorolysis, in the absence of EDTA, no variation in the formation of Glc-I-P was detected by adding 3 mM ATP, 2 mM UTP, 40 mM imidazole, 20 mM MnCI~, 4 mM MgC12, 20 mM glucose, 20 mM sodium pyrophosphate, 1.8 mM UDP, 4 mM EDTA and 20 mM sorbitol; with 3 mM UMP an inhibition of about 3 ° ~o was observed.
It appears from the data shown in Table I that the enzyme reported in this paper is clearly distinguishable from laminaribiose phosphorylase. The ratio of activities of the two enzymes remains rather constant during the three first steps of purification; but most of the laminaribiose phosphorylase is obtained in the fraction eluted with 5 mM sodium pyrophosphate, while a concn, of IO mM is necessary to obtain the highest activity of fl-I,3-oligoglucan phosphorylase. These data are in apparent contradiction with those reported previously by GOLDEMBERG, MARECHAL AND DE SOUZA 1, who found that the ratio of enzymic activity between laminaritriose and laminaribiose (Eqn. I, left to right) as substrates remained quite constant during the different steps of purification. Probably this was due to the fact that the assays were carried out with old enzyme preparation and in the absence of mercaptoethanol. As can be seen in Fig. 4 only a minute amount of Pi was liberated from Glc-I-P when fi-I,3-oligoglucan phosphorylase was assayed in the absence of-SH donors.
It is difficult to ascertain the specificity of each enzyme. Both of them can use almost the same acceptors and form fl-i,3-oligosaccharides from glucose and Glc-I-P, but they show different kinetic behavior. Thus fl-I,3-oligoglucan phosphorylase forms higher oligosaccharides from IO mM laminaribiose, laminaritriose and laminaritetraose, about twice as fast as from glucose at the same concentration (Table V). Laminaribiose phosphorylase, on the contrary, synthesizes the same oligosaccharides from IO mM glucose at a 3-4-fold higher rate than from the di-, tri-and tetrasaccharide 1.
It remains to be determined whether laminaribiose phosphorylase can phosphorolyze laminaritriose or higher/5-I,3-oligosaccharides, or whether the action was due to a contamination with /5-I,3-oligoglucan phosphorylase. On the other hand, the latter enzyme phosphorolyzes laminaribiose but no definite proofs were obtained in this paper as to whether this effect is due to a contamination with laminaribiose phosphorylase, as might be suspected from the separation methods. The next paper deals with comparative studies on both enzymes in order to gain further insight into this problem.
